Other bone turnover markers, such as collagen peptides, have been studied, though no significant differences were found between ALP, BALP, and collagen peptide levels when assessing the presence and extent of pagetic bone changes (meta-analysis) [ ]. 7. Medical Therapy Strategies There have been no updates to therapeutic management guidelines since the 2019 UK Guidelines, which recommend bisphosphonates as the first-line treatment for PDB, based on findings from randomized controlled trials [ , ]. Zoledronic acid shows superior efficacy in managing bone pain compared to pamidronate, alendronate, and risedronate [ ]. Currently, no evidence supports the idea that bisphosphonates improve quality of life, prevent fractures, slow hearing loss progression, or prevent/treat deformities associated with PDB [ , ]. Bisphosphonates in general and nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NCBs) in particular effectively reduce bone turnover, as evidenced by ALP normalization. Among NCBs, zoledronic acid is most effective, showing longer-lasting control over ALP levels when administered as a single 5 mg intravenous dose, maintaining ALP normalization for up to 5 years [ ]. Bisphosphonate treatment aims to control bone pain and normalize ALP. The results of treating asymptomatic patients to prevent complications remain inconclusive. For patients unable to use bisphosphonates, calcitonin provides an alternative for short-term pain relief and ALP reduction, though it is more costly and linked to an increased risk of cancer with long-term use; thus, it is recommended only for short-term use [ ]. Denosumab has no current support as an effective treatment for PDB, so its use is not advised [ ]. Anabolic agents, such as teriparatide, are contraindicated for PDB, even after the FDA’s removal of the boxed warning of osteosarcoma risk [ , ]. For pain management in symptomatic patients, analgesics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and anti-neuropathic medications are commonly prescribed, though none have been specifically studied for PDB pain management [ ]. 8. Follow-Up Monitoring is particularly important for PDB patients who have received antipagetic therapy, with an initial assessment of response after three and six months via ALP measurements. If results are satisfactory, semi-annual or annual monitoring may suffice (practice guidelines) [ , ]. Additionally, annual radiographic evaluations are recommended for osteolytic lesions to assess for improvement or worsening following treatment. In asymptomatic, untreated patients, regular ALP monitoring helps evaluate disease progression, even in monostotic cases or cases with normal ALP levels. BALP testing can also assist in such evaluations [ ]. 9. Prognosis Although the most recent guidelines (2019 UK Guidelines) indicate that there is no clear evidence that specific treatments slow disease progression or prevent complications, early diagnosis and access to treatments before severe complications develop may improve prognosis [ ]. Early diagnosis as a basis for effective disease management has encouraged the dissemination of practical information for primary care published in 2020 in the UK and the US [ , ]. J.R. Naihid and K. Jude provide a diagnostic flowchart for suspected PDB cases, as shown in [ ]; C. Nairn and S.H. Ralston offer guidance on referring patients to secondary care, as shown in [ ]; and the American Academy of Family Physicians has released patient information titled “Paget Disease of Bone: What You Should Know,” available online at https://www.aafp.org . Although PDB incidence and severity appear to be decreasing in high-prevalence populations, interest in the disease persists. These shifts in epidemiology may warrant continued research to better understand its etiopathogenesis [ ]. 10. The CARHES study (Cardiovascular Risk in Renal Patients of the Health Examination Survey) reported a CKD prevalence of 6.3% in Italy. According to data from the Italian Institute of Statistics (ISTAT) [ ], in January 2025, the population aged over 50 years in the province of Grosseto (Tuscany—central Italy) numbered 111,252 people. This calculation does not consider CKD cases potentially resulting from the complications of PDB. Because of the lack of data, a correct estimate cannot be made, though such data could be obtained from cross-sectional or cohort studies. To date, only 16 cases involving both PDB and CKD have been documented ( ) [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. A prospective study was conducted in 21 patients over seventy years of age undergoing dialysis, hemodialysis, or chronic ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) to assess the presence of skeletal alterations. The study reported pagetic lesions in 5% of cases, along with other more frequent lesions [ ]. The coexistence of these two conditions may simply reflect their prevalence in the population; however, in some cases, the complications of PDB can cause CKD. Long-lasting hypercalcemia, nephrolithiasis, and obstructive tubulopathy from crystal precipitation are potential causes of CKD in PDB patients. Hypercalcemia may result from immobility in severe cases or from vitamin D and calcium therapy. PDB itself is an independent risk factor for nephrolithiasis (NL), as metabolic remission (normal ALP) in PDB patients still doubles the incidence of stone formation compared to in controls [ ]. Cardiovascular risk factors linked to PDB, such as arterial hypertension and valvular calcifications, increase the likelihood of heart failure, further complicating renal health [ ]. sHPT is a common condition in CKD patients, even in the early stages of disease, and it may mask asymptomatic forms of PDB with ALP levels in the normal range since it induces the nephrologist not to proceed with further investigations, limiting the action to the control of sHPT by means of Vit D/Vit D analogs, calcimimetics and if necessary calcium supplements after adequate control of phosphatemia. Hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, typical alterations of sHPT in the advanced stages of CKD, lead to cardiac and vascular calcifications [ ]. These calcifications, which may also occur as a result of the therapy used to treat metabolic bone disease in CKD (CKD-MBD), contribute to reducing the survival of CKD patients [ , ]. Both PDB and CKD patients have increased mortality and vascular and cardiac calcifications as a result of abnormal bone remodeling. Research Questions and Considerations in Relation to the Presence of References in the Literature on the Coexistence of CKD in Patients with PDB Why is this association seldom discussed? Would a questionnaire regarding the coexistence of the two diseases addressed to general practitioners and nephrologists be of any use? How many PDB patients develop CKD as a complication? In the studies conducted, did the evaluation of sHPT data take into account the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (by age, sex, and body weight) of patients with PDB? Is it possible that sHPT is partly due to the underestimated coexistence of early or moderate stages of CKD? 11. Pharmacological Management Challenges in CKD Patients with PDB The presence of CKD complicates the treatment of PDB, as antipagetic drugs are primarily excreted through the kidneys via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion [ , ]. As CKD progresses, drug concentrations can increase in the blood and bone, resulting in prolonged and excessive skeletal effects. This may worsen CKD-MBD and depress bone turnover, leading to conditions such as osteomalacia, mixed uremic osteodystrophy, and adynamic bone disease (ABD) [ ]. Bisphosphonate nephrotoxicity, especially from intravenous administration, is known to potentially induce acute renal failure (ARF) due to glomerular sclerosis and acute tubular necrosis. Recovery from ARF is variable, with some patients experiencing partial, full, or no recovery of renal function after stopping the drug (as reported in one review and three cases) [ , ]. Nephrotoxicity risk is dose-dependent and influenced by the infusion rate; hence, spacing out doses is recommended [ ]. Given these risks, bisphosphonates are generally contraindicated when GFR falls below 35–30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 [ , ]. Research indicates that osteoporosis treatments with bisphosphonates are managed similarly in CKD and non-CKD patients in primary care, despite contraindications for low GFR and the specifics of CKD-MBD [ ]. For dialysis patients, a new avenue might become available, as clodronate, pamidronate, and ibandronate are dialyzable and may be feasible options, though dedicated studies on this are needed [ ]. Combining NSAIDs with diuretics or renin–angiotensin system inhibitors (RASIs) may further reduce GFR by affecting glomerular hemodynamics (as reported in a retrospective review of clinical/administrative records) [ ]. Calcium and vitamin D supplements used for both conditions require careful monitoring to avoid hypercalcemia, as reported in the KDIGO guidelines [ ]. lists the pharmacological precautions for patients with CKD. The complex pharmacological approach to PDB, which is due to the contraindications of bisphosphonates in CKD for GFR < 35–30 mL/min/1.73 m in isolated cases (listed in ), has led to the use of denosumab, a drug not mentioned in the guidelines, with reported positive results; however, the data should be considered anecdotal. 12. Considerations for CKD-MBD and Bone Turnover in PDB and CKD Patients Determining the presence or absence of CKD-MBD in patients with both osteoporosis and CKD is crucial, as it helps to differentiate renal osteodystrophy types with high or low bone turnover [ ]. Likewise, identifying CKD-MBD in patients with both CKD and PDB may be necessary. Assessing non-pagetic bone for CKD-related changes may help distinguish among renal osteodystrophy types, with histomorphometric characteristics identifiable by bone biopsy using the TMV classification, which assesses turnover, mineralization, and volume (practice guidelines) [ ]. Knowledge of CKD-MBD is changing: initial studies showed predominant alterations related to high bone turnover. In more recent studies, an increase in normal bone turnover was reported. However, major findings from bone biopsies performed in the USA and Europe (as well as in Turkey, Venezuela, and Brazil) showed lesions from low turnover. Furthermore, an increasing presence of osteoporosis has been documented, which complicates the already complex pathogenesis of CKD-MBD [ ]. summarizes the histological changes observed in the various types of renal osteodystrophy. Kidney transplantation does not solve the problems faced by CKD patients, as the permanence, progression, or evolution of lesions into other types has been documented independently of renal function. Osteoporosis has also been described in post-transplant patients. The causes of these changes could be accredited, at least in part, to the therapies used for CKD-MBD and kidney transplantation [ ]. In CKD G3-G5D patients, bone turnover can be evaluated based on PTH and BALP levels, which help distinguish high or low bone turnover patterns (practice guidelines) [ ]. Because routine biopsies are impractical due to their limited availability and high costs, these biochemical markers can provide insights into bone turnover patterns in patients with CKD and PDB. Importantly, the KDIGO guidelines recommend measuring serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and ALP levels in CKD patients with GFR < 45 mL/min/1.73 m 2 at least once, making this group, in our opinion, also suitable for PDB diagnostic screening ( ). What influence could sHPT in CKD and nephrological therapy used for its control have on PDB outcomes? Could even advanced uremic conditions alone impact PDB? Does the coexistence of the two diseases worsen morbidity and mortality compared to the presence of only one disease? 13. PDB and Kidney Transplantation The interaction between PDB and kidney transplantation is an underexplored area. The KDIGO guidelines for transplant candidates do not list PDB among the absolute or relative contraindications, and evaluations for kidney transplant suitability remain at the discretion of individual transplant teams [ ]. A search on PubMed and Google Scholar revealed only one case report of a monostotic PDB patient deemed unsuitable as a living kidney donor. This patient was excluded from the transplant program due to concerns about potential kidney damage from painkillers and bisphosphonates, which may be required to manage PDB in the future (one case) [ ]. This decision aligns with the precautionary principle, prioritizing donor and recipient safety during selection [ ]. Donor selection criteria encompass not only autoimmune and chronic diseases but also other chronic conditions of uncertain origin [ ]. The above criteria may make PDB a potential concern due to its unknown etiology and lack of curative treatment. Should this principle also be applied in the evaluation of transplant candidates with PDB? Most transplanted kidneys gradually lose function due to rejection, drug toxicity, renal artery stenosis, or ureteral obstruction [ ]. The high frequency of NL found in PDB patients and related complications could also further reduce renal survival. Additionally, the association of PDB with hypertension and vascular and valvular calcifications could increase the already high cardiovascular risk of transplant recipients [ ]. In fact, cardiovascular complications are the main cause of death in kidney transplant recipients [ ]. In the absence of explicit guidance, the arguments presented above regarding the suitability of kidney transplant donors and recipients are based primarily on precautionary principles and isolated cases. Research Questions and Considerations in Relation to the PDB and Kidney Transplantation How many patients eligible for kidney transplant have PDB? How many kidney transplant patients have PDB? If kidney transplant patients with PDB could be identified, would it be possible to evaluate the impact of CKD-MBD on PDB outcomes? Could pre- and post-kidney transplant conditions be used to assess the impact of CKD on PDB outcomes? Could each patient’s post-transplant condition serve as a control group compared to the pre-transplant condition? Do kidney transplant patients with PDB have worse morbidity and mortality outcomes than control groups? 14. Limitations Questions, reflections, and hypotheses have emerged from the examination of this topic and could help in the management of patients suffering from PDB-CKD. Unfortunately, the available data do not allow for definitive conclusions to be drawn to support clinical practice. The most important information could be provided by longitudinal/cross-sectional and multicenter studies. Currently, the few clinical cases summarized in demonstrate the existence of patients with PDB-CKD, although they refer to distant settings and cover a 40-year period. The study by M. Conclusions and Future Directions PDB is not a rare disorder; in the EU, a disease is classified as rare if its prevalence does not exceed 0.05% of the population [ ]. Even the coexistence of PDB and CKD is not a rare phenomenon, given that the estimated prevalence in Italy is at least 0.063%. Despite this, information on the topic is rare. Because effective management of PDB depends on early diagnosis and appropriate treatment planning, active pursuit of a PDB diagnosis by both primary care physicians and nephrologists is encouraged. Furthermore, identifying PDB-CKD patients could allow for a sufficient number of patients to be reached for prospective studies. The chronic kidney disease (CKD) setting may be particularly well suited to exploring PDB because of the shared characteristics of the two conditions, including the reliance on common biochemical markers (e.g., PTH and ALP) for diagnosis and monitoring. Specific attention should be paid to therapeutic choices for patients with reduced glomerular filtration rates (GFRs) to avoid treatment complications. Further, screening for PDB in renal transplant donor and recipient evaluations could contribute to identifying additional cases, as could routine follow-up in transplant patients. Given the similarities of the two populations, sharing data on the association between PDB and CKD could advance our understanding of PDB etiopathogenesis and inform best practices in management. We do not know whether CKD can influence the progression of PDB, and if so, how. In this regard, follow-up of patients with PDB and CKD who have undergone kidney transplantation could provide interesting data on the pre- and post-transplant periods. Above all, and more immediately, attention to the coexistence of the two diseases could improve patient management with personalized choices based on their renal function.

chunks.content: Introduction Maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) is a major renal replacement therapy for patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Owing to the combined effects of the disease and its treatment, MHD patients are at high risk for falls, with reported incidence (12–49%) approximately twice that of the community-dwelling population [ ]. Falls can result in delayed dialysis, physical injury, disability, loss of independence, reduced quality of life, and increased healthcare burden [ , ]. Notably, patients who sustain a hip fracture after a fall face a fourfold increase in one-year mortality, and those without fractures have a 60% higher one-year mortality risk, compared with non-fallers [ ]. Previous studies indicate that falls in MHD patients arise from a complex interplay of physiological, environmental, and behavioral factors, including patient-specific conditions, treatment-related aspects [ ], and environmental hazards [ ]. The multifaceted nature of these risk factors in home settings poses significant challenges for accurately predicting falls. The Person-Environment-Occupation (PEO) model provides a patient-centered theoretical framework based on the concept of person-environment fit [ ], making it highly suitable for multidimensional fall-risk assessment. Although several studies have examined risk factors for falls in MHD patients [ , ], most primarily focus on physiological and treatment-related factors, often neglecting environmental risks in home settings. International literature and guidance from Australia [ ], the United States [ ], and Europe [ , ] support attention to environmental hazards in fall prevention. Consequently, omitting environmental factors may reduce model predictive accuracy in real-world home settings. This study applied the PEO framework to identify home fall-risk factors in MHD patients across three dimensions: personal factors, environmental conditions, and daily activities. We then developed a preliminary Random Forest (RF) model to assess its internal performance and explore its potential utility for individualized fall-risk stratification. A preliminary version of this work has been posted as a preprint [ ]. Methodology Study population This single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with ESRD receiving maintenance hemodialysis. The cohort was established using data from patients who had undergone MHD at our hemodialysis center before January 1, 2024, and who met the following inclusion criteria: (1) diagnosis of ESRD and receipt of MHD treatment; (2) regular hemodialysis for ≥ 3 months; and (3) ability to ambulate independently or with a walking aid. Exclusion criteria were (1) comorbid cardiopulmonary failure or other severe systemic diseases; (2) falls attributable to acute medical events; and (3) visual, hearing, or speech impairments. Patients with visual, hearing, or speech impairments were excluded because these conditions could substantially interfere with questionnaire completion and independent environmental assessment in this retrospective design. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Army Medical University (Approval No.: 2024-110-02). This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations. Written informed consent was obtained from all the participants. Data collection Data were collected from two primary sources for comprehensiveness and accuracy. First, clinical and laboratory data, including laboratory parameters, medication records, and documented comorbidities, were extracted from the hospital’s clinical information system. Second, patient-reported and environmental data were obtained via a structured electronic questionnaire administered using the Tencent Questionnaire mini-program on WeChat. This questionnaire was completed by patients themselves during a scheduled visit to the hemodialysis center, with a research nurse present to provide clarification if needed, thereby ensuring data completeness and quality. Demographic variables, assessment of the home environment, and information on daily activities were collected through this self-reported questionnaire. Consequently, variables pertaining to the Environment and Occupation dimensions of the PEO framework were primarily sourced from this questionnaire. Intradialytic hypotension (IDH) was defined as a decrease in systolic blood pressure ≥ 20 mmHg or a drop in mean arterial pressure ≥ 10 mmHg, accompanied by symptoms requiring clinical intervention [ ]. For the purpose of this study, a positive “history of IDH” was assigned if a patient had experienced at least one such episode within the 12 months preceding the baseline assessment (i.e. on or after January 1, 2023). History of IDH was defined as the occurrence of at least one IDH episode within the 12 months prior to baseline. Home environment variables and data on daily activities reflected the patient’s status at this baseline assessment. Data preceding this date were used to define predictors, ensuring temporal precedence over the outcome events collected during 2024. Data on fall events occurring between January 1 and December 31, 2024, were collected retrospectively. During a dedicated data collection phase, the responsible dialysis unit nurses administered the study questionnaire (hosted on the Tencent Questionnaire platform) to each patient during their routine hemodialysis session. The questionnaire included a specific, standardized item to ascertain home falls during the defined outcome period. To enhance accuracy and complement patient recall, the electronic medical records of all participants for the corresponding period were also reviewed to identify any documented fall-related injuries or healthcare visits. All reported or recorded potential fall events were then verified by two independent researchers (LXY and XZ) against the study definition. Events confirmed through this verification process were classified as outcome events. The home environment was defined according to the World Health Organization [ ] spatial integrity criteria, referring to a functionally isolated residential unit with a net area per capita of ≥ 8 m 2 and natural ventilation. The primary outcome, fall at home, was defined as any fall occurring in the home environment between January 1 and December 31, 2024. The outcome was treated as binary. Data on fall severity were not systematically collected, as the study focused on predicting the occurrence of any fall. To perform preliminary feature selection and reduce model dimensionality, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression was employed. This method uses L1 regularization to shrink coefficients of irrelevant variables to zero, thereby retaining key predictors and reducing statistical burden, and has been shown to outperform traditional univariate screening methods [ ]. All continuous predictor variables were standardized (z-score) prior to LASSO regression. The optimal regularization parameter (λ = 0.0239) was selected via 10-fold cross-validation based on the minimum mean-squared error. Statistical analysis Data normality was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Normally distributed data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, and non-normally distributed data as median with interquartile range. Categorical variables were summarized as counts (percentages). Continuous variables were compared using Student’s t -test or the Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate, and categorical variables using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and R software version 4.5.1. A two-sided p -value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. Model development and validation The dataset was partitioned using stratified random sampling, with the outcome variable as the stratification factor to maintain consistent proportions of fall events between training and test sets. Overall, 70% of patients were allocated to the training set for model development, and the remaining 30% to an independent internal test set for validation. After data splitting, SMOTE was applied exclusively to the training set to address class imbalance by generating synthetic minority-class samples; no resampling was performed in the test set. The Random Forest model was developed using the randomForest package in R. Hyperparameters were optimized via 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. Based on the highest cross-validated area under the curve (AUC), the final model used mtry = 3 (the number of variables randomly sampled as candidates at each split) and ntree = 500. A fixed random seed was set to ensure reproducibility of the results. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the curve (AUC) parameters. Decision curve analysis was performed on the test set by using the rmda package, with net benefit rates and 95% confidence intervals estimated from 1,000 bootstrap samples ( ). This test set represented a hold-out internal validation dataset rather than an external or temporal validation cohort. The study cohort was randomly divided into training and test sets at a 7:3 ratio. The incidence of falls in the home environment did not significantly differ between the two sets ( p = 1.00, ), confirming the appropriateness of the random partitioning. The original training set included 255 patients, of whom 45 (17.65%) experienced home falls and 210 (82.35%) did not. To address class imbalance, SMOTE was applied to generate synthetic samples for the minority class, producing a balanced training dataset of 390 samples, with fall events increased threefold ( n = 180). Feature selection using LASSO regression was performed exclusively on the training set to develop the predictive model, whereas the independent test set was reserved for internal validation. The feature selection results from the LASSO regression model ( and ) indicated that the optimal regularization parameter λ , determined via 10-fold cross-validation, was 0.0239. This process identified six key predictors from an initial set of 28 variables. The Random Forest model demonstrated excellent discriminative performance on the independent internal test set, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.938 ( ). The calibration curve for the predictive model is presented in . The RF model demonstrated a mean absolute error of 0.050, indicating minimal prediction bias, and a Brier score of 0.077, which is substantially lower than the baseline value of 0.16. These findings suggest good internal calibration and discrimination of the RF model. Variable importance, based on the mean decrease in Gini impurity ( ), revealed the following six most influential predictors, in descending order: history of falls, serum potassium level, use of walking aids, absence of anti-slip devices in bathrooms, IDH, and history of diabetes mellitus. Based on the confusion matrix in the internal test set ( ), the model’s accuracy was 0.909 (95% CI: 0.842–0.956). It showed high sensitivity (0.922, 95% CI: 0.749–0.990) while maintaining good specificity (0.850, 95% CI: 0.765–0.914). Additional metrics included a precision of 0.965, recall of 0.922, and an F1-score of 0.943. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis was performed to interpret the output of the optimal RF model at the individual level. The summary plot ( ) illustrates both the direction and magnitude of the six most predictive features. Higher SHAP values indicate stronger contributions toward increased fall risk. Consistent with the feature importance ranking, “history of falls” emerged as the strongest positive predictor, demonstrating the highest mean absolute SHAP value. “Absence of anti-slip devices in bathrooms” and “use of walking aids” were also found to be significant risk factors, with higher feature values corresponding to higher SHAP values. Notably, higher serum potassium levels were associated with negative SHAP values, indicating an inverse contribution to predicted fall risk within the model. Discussion This study developed and internally validated a machine learning model to predict the risk of falls at home in MHD patients. A key strength of this study is the integration of the Person-Environment-Occupation (PEO) framework, which enabled the inclusion of environmental hazards—an important but often underrepresented dimension in existing fall-risk models for MHD patients. The resulting Random Forest model showed promising internal discriminative performance (AUC 0.938), suggesting that integrating environmental factors within the PEO framework may enhance multidimensional home fall-risk assessment in MHD patients. Although feature selection, cross-validation, and an internal hold-out test set were used, the modest number of fall events and the use of SMOTE indicate that overfitting cannot be excluded. Therefore, the present model should be regarded as preliminary and internally validated rather than definitive. RF was selected because it can accommodate non-linear associations and interactions that are common in clinical data [ ]. In the present study, it provided an interpretable framework for preliminary risk estimation, although its performance should be confirmed in larger externally validated cohorts. The variable importance ranking derived from the RF model ( ) offers an intuitive assessment of the relative contribution of predictors associated with falls in the home environment. The six most influential factors, in descending order, were history of falls, serum potassium level, use of walking aids, absence of anti-slip devices in bathrooms, IDH, and history of diabetes mellitus. A prospective multicenter study by Desmet et al. demonstrated that MHD patients with a history of falls within the past year have a 4.8-fold increased risk of recurrent falls, establishing history of falls as the most significant predictor of falls in the home environment [ ] and supporting its role as a consistently important predictor of fall risk [ ]. The same study also reported a 67% increase in fall risk among users of walking aids. Therefore, MHD patients with a history of falls may merit closer clinical attention and individualized fall-prevention assessment. Walking aid use may also help identify patients who warrant assessment of device suitability and mobility support. Serum potassium emerged as an important predictor in the model, with higher values showing an inverse association with predicted fall risk in this cohort. This finding should be interpreted with considerable caution. First, the association is observational and does not imply a causal protective effect. Second, serum potassium was measured at a single pre-baseline time point and may not capture longitudinal exposure or dialysis-related fluctuations. Third, residual confounding cannot be excluded, including confounding by nutritional status, dialysis prescription, frailty, or overall clinical condition. A possible explanation is that lower potassium levels may be associated with impaired neuromuscular function in some MHD patients [ , ]; however, this interpretation remains speculative. Accordingly, these results should not be used to alter potassium management targets. Future prospective studies should further examine the robustness and possible non-linearity of this association. To our knowledge, few studies have identified the absence of anti-slip devices in bathrooms as a predictor of home falls in MHD patients. This environmental factor may contribute to fall risk in patients with existing physiological vulnerabilities. One possible explanation is the interaction between post-dialysis gait instability and slippery surfaces, which may increase the risk of slipping. IDH can also lead to inadequate cerebral perfusion, causing ischemic damage to vestibular nuclei and postural control disorders that may persist for up to 72 h [ ]. Repeated hypotensive episodes may further cause capillary rarefaction in lower-limb muscles, delaying strength recovery [ ]. Accordingly, bathroom safety may represent a potentially modifiable target for fall prevention, and practical measures such as anti-slip devices or grab bars may be considered where appropriate. Patients with recurrent IDH may warrant closer hemodynamic monitoring, and dialysis-related volume management may require further optimization [ ]. The retrospective nature of fall ascertainment introduces potential recall bias. To mitigate this, we implemented a two-step verification process: first, falls were reported via a structured questionnaire administered by a research nurse during a routine dialysis session, which may have enhanced recall through personal interaction; second, we cross-referenced all reported falls with electronic medical records to identify any fall-related injuries or healthcare visits. Despite these efforts, some falls may have been missed or misclassified, particularly those not resulting in injury. Therefore, some degree of outcome underascertainment likely remained. Future prospective studies with real-time fall diaries or wearable sensors would provide more accurate ascertainment and reduce recall bias. The model was developed and validated solely within a single-center, retrospective cohort of Chinese MHD patients. Without external validation in independent, multi-center, or multi-ethnic populations, firm conclusions regarding the model’s transportability cannot be drawn. Future studies should prioritize external validation across diverse geographic regions and healthcare settings to assess generalizability. Additionally, prospective designs with standardized data collection would enhance robustness and allow for temporal validation. Beyond global feature importance, our SHAP analysis provided instance-level insights by quantifying each feature’s contribution magnitude and its consistent directional effect on fall risk. This interpretability may facilitate individualized understanding of model predictions at the patient level. Decision curve analysis was used to evaluate the clinical net benefit of the model across a range of threshold probabilities [ ]. In this internal dataset, the decision curve analysis indicated that a threshold probability of 3% may represent the point above which preventive interventions could be considered. In the present study, the model provided a net benefit of 0.175, corresponding to correctly identifying 17.5 additional fallers per 100 patients compared with a “no intervention” strategy, without causing overtreatment. The RF model demonstrated positive net benefit across threshold probabilities of 3–76% and 91–96%, with clinical utility markedly superior to both “intervene all” and “intervene none” strategies ( ). Consequently, the model may have potential value for preliminary risk stratification in this internal dataset, although external validation is required before routine use. The model also maintained positive net benefit at thresholds up to 96%, although the relevance of this finding to high-risk preference scenarios remains exploratory [ ]. The interruption in the decision curve between 76 and 91% primarily reflects the underrepresentation of medium-risk patients in the training cohort. Therefore, predictions within this range should be interpreted cautiously and considered alongside comprehensive clinical assessment. If externally validated, the model may eventually be integrated into routine dialysis assessments as a preliminary screening aid. At present, however, its role should remain exploratory, and any high-risk classification should be interpreted alongside comprehensive clinical assessment rather than used in isolation. By incorporating the PEO framework into home fall-risk prediction in MHD patients, this study provides a preliminary multidimensional perspective on home risk assessment. This study has limitations that must be considered when interpreting its findings. First, regarding generalizability, the model was developed and validated solely within a single-center, retrospective cohort of Chinese MHD patients. The most significant constraint arising from this design is the lack of external validation. Without validation in independent, multi-center, or multi-ethnic populations, firm conclusions regarding the model’s transportability to other healthcare settings cannot be drawn. Second, inherent to the retrospective design are potential biases. As discussed above, recall bias may affect fall ascertainment despite our verification efforts. Additionally, the deliberate exclusion of patients with visual or hearing impairments, while intended to control for specific severe comorbidities, may limit the model’s applicability and likely result in an underestimation of fall risk in the broader MHD population. The model also provides a static risk estimate over a fixed 12-month horizon and does not account for the dynamic progression of risk factors over time, highlighting a need for research into updatable, shorter-term prediction frameworks. Additionally, our outcome was binary, and data on fall severity (e.g. resulting injury) were not systematically captured; thus, the model predicts the occurrence but not the potential clinical burden of a fall. Finally, due to sample size constraints, we did not perform subgroup analyses (e.g. by age or dialysis vintage) to explore performance heterogeneity, which should be addressed in future, larger studies. Conclusion In summary, we developed a preliminary RF-based model within the PEO framework for estimating home fall risk in MHD patients. The model identified several clinically relevant person-, environment-, and occupation-related factors and showed promising internal performance in this single-center cohort. However, because of the retrospective design, self-reported environmental data, exclusion of sensory-impaired patients, and lack of external validation, these findings should be considered exploratory. External validation in independent multicenter cohorts and prospective studies with real-time fall monitoring and more objective environmental assessment are needed before clinical implementation.
